speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This conversation with Walt Curran took place at his home in Genesee on March 17th, 1976. The interviewer was Sam Schrager. Right onto the reservation.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah, I think the folks moved up here in 1902, about that little place. And they lived there until 1908. And we moved out on the reservation and I grew up there and we stayed there until 1929 out on the farm.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where was it on the reservation?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Out here near top of Coyote Grade. You come up Coyote heavy anytime? Well after you break up on top, coming in. You see the new grade don't come now like it used to. It used to come around over the hills in the farmland. There, and it went right through the farm. We had Indian land, dad rented land from the Indians. And so it made sense, you know, for the farm country out in there, all that rimrock out there is the choice farmland.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What makes it so good? Is it because it's kind of lower than it is here?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: No, not too much. Not too much. It's just an awful good, well-off farmland around here is excellent farmland. But that rim rock out there is, of course, maybe just a little prejudice. I grew up out there. That was in my home. I grew up all the time I was growing up.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, had your father, he had farmed before he went and farmed there? He'd been a farmer before?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh yeah, he was a farmer over at [inaudible]. And then he was up here and the family grew up. And then dad and my brother farmed out there with Fred Nagel, an old timer around here. And then my brother got out of it. And then dad and I farmed together out there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, how did that work? How could you go about renting the Indian land?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: You had to go through the Indian agency in Lapwai. They had the agency control the leasing of the Indian land. And, well, I guess some of the agency buildings are down there yet, and I guess they still have some of the agency there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what kind of a setup was it? Was it a long-term lease or half a year?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, you could get a three-year or five-year lease. Whatever you wanted. And so you had so much rent in each year, you know. You paid so much nacre rent. And that way you had your lease for three or five years, whatever you wanted. Whatever the Indian wanted to let you have through the agency there. And so that worked out pretty good. We had 160 farmland rented, or Indian land rented, besides 240 of our own. And that was back in the old horse days for me, before tractors come in. But they were just coming in when we left the reservation and moved over to Cote. We still farm the horses.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you need much stock to farm with it?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, yes. We started to get up and down. I went to Hampton, just a ranch. We had a roofing ranch. They were a big farm. They run a lot of stock. The average small farmer, they had about, we had about Colts and all, about maybe 20 head of horses. That's about the average little farmer. They had Colts and work horses and saddle horses, stuff like that. And we had some cattle and kind of diversified farming. So it kept us busy.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there a place to live when you moved over there? Was there a place on the...

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, yes. We moved out, it was on Indian land. Well, all the places we lived out here, until Dad bought that 240 of the Connor Ranch. It was all Indian land around us there, all going to the Connors, Corbett's, and all that down there. Matthews, Williams, all down this long central grade there. It was all Indian land. But now it's been bought up by the individuals. There's still some out there yet. But it's being pretty well bought up now.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it readily available then? Could you get it easily? Was there a lot of demand for it?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: There was a lot of demand. You got it by kind of bidding on land through the agency. The highest bidder would usually get it, unless the Indian had to say so himself. We rented George Peale Potallic's land there for nine years, but he was just a wonderful old Indian, honest as they come. He wanted us to have it, we just kept it until we left the reservation. Most of the old Indians that used to be around when I was a boy out there is all passed on now. It's all younger ones now. Family descendants have got the land, what's left there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was George Peale Potallic like? I've heard that he was a really fine man, as you say.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, at one time I guess he was chief of the Nez Perce tribe. He was a nephew of Chief Joseph. So was this. You've heard of this famous Brompet writer, Jackson Sundown? Well, he was also a nephew of Chief Joseph. They were cousins, Jackson Sundown and Pio Potallic. I knew them old fellows. He was only four years old, no doubt. The old fellows that come to town on their saddle horses, old Matt Johnny Matthews and Carl's, all of them old fellows come by where we lived. I really got acquainted with them. Every time they'd come to town and come back by, they'd always have me some candy or gum or something. The old fellows and I, we were pretty good friends. And then I grew up among them and they kept... But they're all gone now. Really, I don't know who all owns the land now.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, back then when those guys were... What would they do? How would they pass the time then?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, hunting, fishing. Gardening. Some of them raised gardens. Some had some horses.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Sometimes they'd go camping or something, you know, they'd travel around.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah. And they lived on what they got off their farmland for the rent.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That was enough for them to give them. Yeah.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: They got so, some of them got so they'd pretty much draw up their rent ahead of time, but this old fellow we rented from old Pio Potallic, he almost never drawed a heck of a lot. He just lived on what he... If he needed something, he'd come and get it. I imagine over... I don't think he ever drawed over $50 a year on these ranches at any time. And he got by, him and his wife lived... Well, it's a house just as you hit the river there on Coyote Grade, just as you hit the highway there on the river. He had a little house back up on the point there. And he had a nice little place. He raised good gardens. He liked to hunt fish. They all seemed to like that, you know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yeah, they do. I think it was him that I heard about that used to camp up around Bovill.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah, he used to go up in there and up on the Clearwater. First time I ever went deer hunting with that old fellow. We took his team of horses and an old pack. We went up and we went up through Kendrick, up in his timber, much in there. And we went up in there and we camped one night. Within the day we went up and the next day evening we had a deer in an elk apiece. The old fellow, he was a... He'd go through that timber, you'd never hear him go. He used to sneak up on them. But he was a great hunter.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How old were you about then, just guessing?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, I was... I imagine maybe 1920s, early 20s.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was he teaching you how to hunt?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh yes. Yeah, he showed me a lot of things about still hunting and everything.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Still hunting?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh yeah, that's... You just find your good game trail and back off. He showed me how to do that. Just wait for your game to get to traveling. They'd come through this game trail and you'd get them. Otherwise he'd sneak through that timber. It's so quiet you couldn't even hear him. He'd just get through there and lots of times he'd walk right up on game in the timber there. Different than they do nowadays.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That sure sounds different than the way I learned to hunt.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh yes. Yeah, of course. It seemed like them Indians had a way of doing it. They sure were... Great hunters. The wonderful things they used to make with their beautiful lives.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yeah. Things they used to make?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah, beadwork. Beadwork. Oh, they were great for making beads. And gloves. They were great to make these blue skin gloves and jackets and moccasins. You see, they made their clothes out of all the animal hides they know of these. Well, most of them. Is that the dog or the dog? I don't know. But anyway, they'd take these little small beads, different colors, and they'd make the prettiest flowers on these gloves and the beadwork bags and stuff and their jackets. They'd bead on that. They were the finest artists going for that. See, they made all their clothes and stuff from the animal hides. They never wasted a thing when they got an animal. They did everything they could.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've seen that at Lapwai, you know, at the Indian dances. God, that must be a lot of the old work that they still have.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Here a while back, some of the old time Indian ladies, they was putting on classes learning to the young ones how to do that down there, how to make baskets and buckskin stuff. It was showing them, learning them the trade like the old fellows used to, the old Indians. And they were great artists at that. No, not Mark. Woody Vart?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But, you know, it's kind of funny that nowadays you wouldn't think of, well, maybe that somebody who is like an Indian would really go down with trouble with a white boy, you know, to teach him how to make good hearts.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, I'll tell you. If they were a friend to you, they'd do anything to help you. If they hated you, they'd do it the other way. If they were an enemy, what? But they'd do anything in the world for you if they liked you. Yeah, they were great friends of ours out there. The folks, a lot of them old timers, they'd almost stop the folks. Mother-in-law would raise a big garden and they'd come through. Camp there, some had money, some didn't. She never refused eggs, butter, garden stuff. They'd come back from Huckleberry and Mother-in-law would always get her five or six gallons of Huckleberries. They'd always bring her out a bunch of Huckleberries, them old Indian ladies. And the same way with fishing, they'd go fishing down on the river and they'd bring us fish up there. Fresh fish. No, if they liked you, boy, they'd do anything for you.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, it sounds like they liked you, they must have liked you. Why do you think they liked you? Was it because you shared like that?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, yes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The gift that you had?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: We always treated them right and we never, we always, well, treated them just on the equal with the other people and they appreciated it. And like that. I never was around them. I was scared to death of them, but then, you know, they never hurt me. But, you know, just kids, you know, now I'm not used to it. After that, then it didn't bother me anymore. But they were... Never was around them like you are now. You treat them, you treat an Indian right, then. You treat your right. You betcha. They're good friends. I still got a lot of friends down there around Lapwai, even their younger ones.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were there some people that didn't treat them well in those days?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, I don't know. I couldn't say that because I never was around them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, just when you say if they didn't like you, they really didn't like you.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, if you'd done something to them to make them mad, well, they were mad. And something like that. If you'd done them dirt or something, and something that hurt them, why, no, they didn't anymore do we. But if you just treat them right and you do them a favor, and they do you one favor, they wouldn't take no back.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about Jackson Sundance? What kind of guy was he?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: He was a fine old Indian. And boy, he was one of the best bronc riders. He used to come up out there, well, we lived on the reservation back in the teens and 20s, they'd have the stop shows here and the rodeo. And he would come up and him and his wife and family would camp out there. And he'd come in here to the show during the day and then back out to his camp. And he was a fine old fella, old Jackson was. Yes sir. He was just one of the better ones.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: As far as Wright goes, I guess I've heard he was all over the country. Wasn't he in Pendleton?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: He won the World Championship in Pendleton down there. Yeah. Oh, he was a dandy. And the nicest old Indian to be around you ever seen. I ever saw him, although I heard of him. He was just Pio Potallic, George Pio Potallic. He was the finest old Indian you could be around.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Somebody told me about Pio Potallic, how considerate he was. He'd gone and stayed at their place and he was doing some round of work with them. And he was the only one that really said, well, your cooking was great. I enjoyed the hospitality.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: He used to get up in the morning in a little place there on the river, go out and take a swim in the Clearwater, I thought it was in the late fall, floating ice. Get out, get on his little horse and come up to the ranch there, and he'd get up there the time we were having breakfast and have breakfast with us. And he'd visit a while, take off again back for the river. He used to make jerky and bring it to us. He was a very considerate old fellow.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was he an old man at this time when he was diving in the river and swimming around?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yes, he was around the late 60s and 70s in there. He always took a homey swim in the Clearwater. I don't remember him, I never saw him. You bet.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did Jackson's son and dad ever teach you anything about riding?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, he gave me quite a few pointers. Of course, I was a dumb kid growing up about that time. I learned a lot from Jackson.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yeah, I guess he was a funny, funny boy.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Of course, I wasn't as lucky. He'd ride him and I'd get fooling around and get bucked off.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you interested in that riding?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yes, I liked it. I liked it. I used to break horses in the winter. In the summertime, of course, I was too busy with the farm. We'd farm by horses. I'd have two or three sad horses around. But I liked messing around with horses and cattle. Real good.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This broad riding that you did, was there much rodeoing around here? Oh, yes. Did you keep to have a chance to learn that kind of stuff in those days?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah, you'd take all the farm kids they used to get. Well, they had cattle and stuff. Of course, they'd get out and ride calves and stuff more when they were on the farm. They all had an idea that they wanted to ride, so they'd get out and do it themselves. Sometimes nobody would tell them to just get out and learn it. It was a lot of fun. He did get bucked off. Farming's different now. It's all machine right now instead of the horses. You know, thrash machines and stuff.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did Jackson Sundance ever, I mean, would he fool around on the horses whether or not he was in a rodeo? I mean, would he have his own string or anything?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: No, he had horses, but he never had a rodeo string. He just went and rodeoed in the shovels. Yeah, he'd come up there and camp and come here. They'd always go and camp wherever. He was riding. Put up their teepees, same way. Oh, Lewiston, Pendleton, wherever they had a show, he'd go and ride.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was this Janicey Horse Show, was that a rodeo?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, they had the rodeo in connection with the horse show. At them days, why, they had some fine horses around, draft horses. Then they'd have, oh, maybe the last day of the show, they'd have a rodeo. And everybody had some bucking horses around the country. It wasn't at that time, there really wasn't any special rodeo strings. Everybody out in the country had horses. And if they had a horse that they thought was a good bucking horse, why, they'd bring him in and they'd try him out. They'd have the show that way. But they never hired a string like they do, or a string of horses like they do at Lewiston and around to put on the shows.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But that's what Sundance was here for, wouldn't be for the horse show that he'd come here.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, he'd come for the horse show and the bronc riding. He'd, same way at Pendleton, he went down, they had a lot of things there that we didn't have. Of course, now it's commercialized. They have these regular strings that come in.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, did this draw people in from very far?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, yes. All these small town-drawn here would come in. And, oh, we had rodeos here. The Hanna boys used to come in, put on rodeos here. And old Gus Gamble, Chet Sam's had horses, and we all had horses we'd put in with them, put on the show here.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Gus used to do that rodeo in too?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, yeah, he had a bunch of horses out here on the rim, and him and Chet Sam's, they can bring the stock in. So everybody, like I say, had a bucking horse, they'd bring them in. So that made fun for all.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there much fun in it for a guy like Jackson Sundance?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, it all depends on what your purse was for championships. Each little showhouse had probably a different purse, you know. I imagine he had as much as I do now. Oh, no, that's my guess.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know, it doesn't seem to me like they're all that big now either. Some of these guys could ride to certain, the champion and the national champion could maybe have $50,000, which isn't so much compared to other jobs.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, no. Well, for the chances they take and the rough part of it, why, it isn't too much. Of course, nowadays, them days you rode a horse to a finish, now you ride him so many seconds.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You rode him to a finish, what do you mean?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Until the horse quit buttoning.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, yeah?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Mm-hmm. Now they ride him eight seconds, ten seconds, whatever it is, what he's set now.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, how long could a horse keep buttoning them days?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Some of them would go quite a ways. I never stuck with enough of them to go all the way with. No, I don't know. I'm thinking about them. I guess I'll go watch them. Geez. Yeah, they... What a lot of sports. You never know when you're going to get hurt or not.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, you'd better dry out your pride. Did you do much rodeo riding yourself? Did you ever?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, I never rode the shows too much. I was usually... Well, I usually worked as pick-up man or hazer or something like that. I never really rode the shows too much. Sometimes I'd try it. I never had the time to get away to follow the shows. We were on the farm, you know, with that work and stuff. So I never had a chance to get away too much.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you... Were you ever over at the penalty show over there to work in it?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Mm-hmm. Well, I didn't work in it. I went over to that old pill patella one time, and I was just a kid. I rode racehorses, his racehorses, on the show. One year he took me over. I had his two racehorses up keeping them up on the ranch. He took one of them over and took me along with him. We had a good time down there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What's the hazer do? Which guy...

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Hazen? Well, Hazen was on all bulldogging. He's a steer on one side while the dog comes on the other. Sometimes running the stock and bucking the horse. Buck the rider off and run him out. Pick him up and take the saddle off of him. And pick up the rider horse and quit bucking while you run in it. Pick the horse up, snub him up and take the rider off on the back of your horse. Then he's going over. You can just take him back in, take the saddle off of him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It always struck me as a real dangerous game. I guess that's because I've never been much of a rider.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, you never knew what them horses were going to do sometimes. Some of them would try to take you and knock you out of the saddle, and some of them would want to keep on bucking. So you just never knew what the horse was going to do. When you went in there, you just took your chances.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I was just thinking of holding on. How did you do that? When the horse was bucking, what was the way that you learned to...

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, you wouldn't dare pull, grab the saddle horn or they'd disqualify you. You had your bucking reins and your saddle, and you ride with your balance to the horse, over the horse. So it was just... It's a game all with its own. Some get good, some never learn.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wonder where a guy like Sundance, ever, Jackson Sundance, would pick it up.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, he told us when he was a kid, he used to go out and ride buffaloes. Yeah, when he was a kid, see, named Old Peel. And Old Peel was a good rider too, but he never rode a bull sundown. He used to go out and ride buffaloes. He'd take these old bulls with a saddle or a bareback cinch, he didn't make a difference. He did learn it when he was from a kid out that way.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When they had them rodeos, what did they have to go... Nowadays, you know, they got all that... Some of them have a lot of carnival stuff. What did they have to go with them in them days?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Anything special?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Some would have maybe a little carnival and some didn't. They just put on the show in the afternoon. Usually have a ball game in the morning, baseball teams, afternoon, be a rodeo. Sometimes, they'd get a little carnival in. Riding around Ferris Wheel or something like that. Sometimes they had shows.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It really sounds like a...

speaker: Walter Currin
words: It was a lot of fun. It was something to do.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But you say like the horses and stuff in those rodeos, they weren't brought in by the people? I mean, they just didn't like it as now.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: The first one that ever came into the Genesee with a bucking string was George the Hanna Brothers. That was 1929. They came in ahead of time and they kept... Brought in a bunch of horses and anybody had a good bucking horse, they'd try him out. And if he looked like he'd make a good bucker, they'd either buy him or trade him another horse for it to button a bucking horse. So they stuck around here a whole... In the two weeks that way. But the main show they put on was about a three or four day show. It was on over the Fourth of July celebration. They had an awful good string of horses and they were nice fellows to work with. George Hanna, the only one I know of who is at now, he lives down here in the Lewis Northridge someplace. But they don't have the string anymore. He's way up in the 80s now so he's just too dumb to hold for that. But he still mucked his round. He liked stock.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They didn't go all around the country other places?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh yes. Wherever they wanted to contract them to come in with a bucking string, they'd go in.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And that was as a part of the stock show and rodeo that they had?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, yeah. See they quit having the stock shows afterwards but then they had rodeos around in here. I know... I went up with the Hanna Boys. I worked with them here in 29 and then I went up with them to the Riverside Park up there towards Potlatch. They was in here twice, once at Uniontown. Wherever they could... they only would come in and put a show. Why, they'd bring their rodeo stock in and put it on.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I gotta admit I'm really ignorant about bucking horses and all that. You're saying that only some horses would be buckers?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah. Not all of them would be. Maybe they'd come out. Maybe buck once and next time they would quit and they wouldn't do a thing. And a lot of them would just keep on getting worse. That's where the ones they used strings, they liked to get a hold of. Some of them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How well were horses cared for in them days on the farms and the stock?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, it all depended on the individual. Most of them took good care of their stock. And some of them just not quite as good as the others. But they had to because they had to depend on them for their farm work. You see, plowing, seeding, and running a header or a binder or even pulling a combine. Useful combine in the arts. They have a whole... all the way from... Oh, ground full combines.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about the... what was the size of the horses that came?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, they'd run all the way from... all 1200 up to 1600, 1700 pounds. Oh yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they have a lot of different kinds or was there certain...

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, there was... Oh, there was Shires, Belgians, and Perchans were mostly around this country. And sometimes it was just mixed breeds. That was the three main breeds of horses they had around. For the farm work. On the count of the flu epidemic. Well, I was running around out there at the ranch and an old man swing came up. He wouldn't know what I was doing. Monkey ran out of school and I told him I wasn't any. It closed him off, huh? So his daughter was teaching. His daughter Joanna was teaching down on the Coyote Grade School. So he told me to come in and get my books and so I did. And I went and finished the school year down there. There was six of us white kids and eight Indian kids. And that was the size of the school. We had a good little school. She was a real good teacher. Joanna was. She's passed on now. But it was... I had a real good year down there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where'd you been going to school before?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Here in Genesee.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh. What was the difference between a school here and a town and a school in a country like that?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: There wasn't any difference. Only here in town we had our one grade, you know, our two grades. And down there we had all the way from the first to the eighth grade. And we rode a saddle horse. Her brother and I rode from up here on the hill. Then after come spring, why she was boarding down there with a comfort family. So then she used to ride a horse down with us too in the morning until school was out. I know, just the atmosphere being out in the country, you know. I had good school. I don't know when they opened the school. I know the clothes didn't coat them that year too. Well, it was closed in Genesee quite a while. Terrible.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were there many people around here that got the flu?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, everybody had it. We lost several around here. One man and wife both died within just a few hours of each other. Well, there's an awful lot of them died around here. That was the first time I really had here. I think I skipped a dead year if I remember right. Well, I was pretty lucky too that year. But it was bad, real bad. We had the chicken, I mean the measles and chicken parts. Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Munch. Did you get to play Indian games when you went down there?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh yeah, I used to play with the Indian kids down there. Mike Sweeney and I, we was the two boys from up here on the hill. We played with them down there, Indian games and stuff.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What kind of games?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, they had, you get down and play the stick game and stuff like that. The kids, Indian kids, you know. Different little things they had.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Stick game.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah, they played that. I don't remember how the devil we did play it now. And then they played just the same as us kids too, you know. Baseball and things like that. I guess, I don't know. They liked baseball. We played down there. It was Swenson now. He wasn't ever around here.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: No, he's Park and Erie. Uh huh.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: I don't know. No, that was, we had to, she had to go to school. There was Swenson used to live here a year ago, but I guess he was no relative of them. Uh huh. Yeah, if you contact Maylon, he can probably give you a lot more history further back than I can. Because he was born, well he's in his 80s now. And he's an old timer here. Of course, I lived out here in the country. I missed a lot of city life then.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When did you start working on the farm? How old were you when you started?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, I'd say about 11, 12 years old.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you start in on doing?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, driving team, plow team, different things in the field. A lot of kids used to start in the 14th. Helping in the hay, mowing hay, breaking, stuff like that. Yep, they had to do that, I guess, in those things. And when I was going to school, I rode from, well seven mile out to Genesee here. And Saturday, well Dad would be working in the field. My brother, Saturday, I'd take Dad's team in the field, plow team, or whatever he was doing. That's how I got broke into handling horses.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you start with just two horses, or did you start with a whole?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, we had seven or eight head on the gang plow, probably six on a harrow. Two on a mow machine and a rake, stuff like that. So, I drove combine several years with horses around these hills. I went to run push binder, and went to the tractor work.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know, they talk about the Genesee harvests all over this county. No matter where you go, if you go out to Deeree Park, way out there, they say, well, it was... While we were peering up the land, of course, we could... Father worked out at Genesee Harvest.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah, they'd come down here and harvest and work. Oh yes, and then in the old steam thrashing machine days, there were several machines that would come from Troy down in this country. The thrash grain. There was the Swensons, Albert Hall, Seth, all different ones, Holy Flammel. Different fellows that had big thrashing outfits would come down here and thrash the grain. They hit it grain, or the bundle grain, after they started binding.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I mean, there was enough of a market for them to come in from outside with their own machinery?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh yes, well, yeah. All these farmers around here didn't have a thrashing machine of their own, and those fellows would come down. It covered all the way from, I'd say, the worst of the night, all around to Clearwater, to out here to Redjuie. You had all that country in there, you know, thrashed. They hit it and thrashed, and they used to stack the grain and thrash it, and they went to bundles before they hit the combines. You bet, there's a big scope of country and a lot of grain here to thrash. Yeah, it seemed to me that that's what they used to do.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did a lot of people come in from, like, harvest, they were migrant? Oh, migrant? Harvest tramps, you call them?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, yeah, there was a lot of them. A lot of them, they said, come in here, 30, 40 days of harvesting, please. They, oh, there was lots of work here for, you know, crutching labor, and they'd work here until some, and some would stay around, you know, help with the farm work, help with the farming, ones that can handle horses, and such as that, until, well, they get to follow some of these farmers that hire them until they get to follow work now. So there was a lot of work around here then, but... Yeah, there is nothing like that now. That's all gone out now, it's just, machine-reuse has taken it out.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I mean, where were those guys came from?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, all over the country. Some of them went down the lower country, down the river. See, they harvest earlier down there than they do here. They'd start in down there and follow the harvest up clear up into here, and go up here, and then go all north, approach Canada. They'd just follow the harvest as they, as it went out, they'd go someplace else before it was later. They followed it then.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it tricky to farm on the hillsides? Was it fairly steep where you had your land?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Some was, and some wasn't. You just had to work your round out according to your hills. So you'd go around the hills and not have to go up the steep hills and stuff like that. But it wasn't too tricky. Almost in a while, have a wreck, but not too often. It was more so with track to work than it was with horses, because you had all that heavy machinery on there. You had to watch your tractor and your machinery. So it wasn't too bad around here. Everybody seemed to farm the hills in good shape.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did your father have a tough time making a go at it, the early days of farming that he did here?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, no, not too bad. Until, well, I'd say until that depression hit there in 29. Of course, Dad only, well, passed away in 31. That depression was a little bit on the rough side, but we pulled through it after it passed away. That's when we moved back here from Colton. We had the place here, we were just renting over there. So we moved back here, and I worked on farm work and construction and different things. And until, well, I'd say until World War II broke out, things opened up then and been going on pretty good.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When did the depression make itself felt here?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, it started long about in 29, or until, I might say, it was getting a little bit better, I might say, until World War II broke out, which at the end hit us in 41 there at the Pearl Harbor. But then things opened up and it went pretty good then.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there, in 29 when that hit, did that mean there was no, did the bottle fall out of the crop market too?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, yes, it just started going down, prices going down, times got tough.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You couldn't borrow any money, you couldn't do nothing?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: And wheat prices went way down, or like your poultry eggs and stuff, that went way down to nothing. There just wasn't any money, to be truthful about it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, who would be a death?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, we pulled through it all right. I had a wife and then a daughter was born in 32 after I came back up here, and mother was with us, so anyway, we lived through it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever hear them talk about the 93 depression around here?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yes, I heard dad talking about that, but I don't remember all the things he told me. He said it was really tough then too. Yeah, that's when he was farming over in Colton. Before they moved up here. Yeah, that's a picture of how they used to thrash here. That's what they would call an old horsepower rig. They didn't have a new engine at all. They'd go around, they had 10, 12 horses, then they had a tumbling rod run over to the sub-bridge from that, and the horses finished following. Dad, the tallest one in the middle there, dropped his old horsepower on the floor. That's the way they thrashed it, over on farm creek and around.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Is that where that was taken?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah, that's where it came from.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where did he come from before he came out to Colton?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oregon.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Willamette Valley?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: That's where dad came from. That's where dad was born, Willamette Valley. Mother came from Arkansas by covered wagon. Both my granddad's homesteaded over at Colton.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wonder how your father heard about Colton country.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, my granddad just heard about this opening up a new country over in here, both my granddad's, so they just headed for out in this country. Dad and his brothers and my granddad, they brought some bunch of cattle with them over to Colton. Granddad homesteaded by the granddad. Well, granddad Kerns is right there at Colton. Grandpa Luper's is about three mile north.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you have much idea when your father might have gotten there from Western Oregon? He was there in the 80s, you're saying?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh yeah, that was 1878.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He landed in Colton. He would be one of the early people.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh yes, there was no Colton or anything in there. Dad hold the first tickle number into Colton there when they built that one building, a doctor in there. He used to freight from Colfax to Lewiston down the hill there. And no, there was no Colton or anything, just a few settlers around there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He would freight supplies from one to the other?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah, from Colfax down to Lewiston, things like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he ever talk about Vollmer? Because I know Vollmer, he run the bank here and in 1993 he did a lot of foreclosing, the story I've heard.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, that's where I guess, we're the old timers, that's where Vollmer got his start, he had a little bit. Yeah, there used to be a Vollmer bank here. And he had a lot of farmlander still some day, still got some farmlander out here. Some of it's been sold off. Vollmer? Vollmer. Oh yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Not too well liked by a lot of locals.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: I don't know anything about him in that regard.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I'll tell you there, he's got a reputation out of Troy in the same way. Troy was named Vollmer to start with.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah, that was the reason, then they changed it to Troy. Yes. Yeah, you betcha.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever know the Rosensteins? Oh yes.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: I knew the Rosenstein family, they had a store out in the old town of Tennessee and then the town moved while they moved in here. I can remember the Rosenstein family. I think they still have some land out here someplace I think. Yeah, it's the Rosenstein girls. Yeah, I know the old Jake Rosenstein and his wife, Mocks and the girls.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What were they like?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, they were nice old folks I thought. They seemed to be a nice family. I never knew them but then I know they used to speak a little. Oh yes, I can remember the Rosenstein family. Your mother-in-law used to talk about them, I never knew them. Yeah, the Rosenstein family, Follett family.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Who did your family trade with?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: We traded with both, Rosenstein's and Follett's. We kind of divided our trade between the two stores.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They were Jewish, weren't they, the Rosenstein's?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Mm-hmm. Yeah. I never knew anything about them in that regard but I just heard their name. I remember when his mother used to take butter or something in there and the old fellow used to hide it up so nobody would get it. Yeah, they used to do that. She used to make homemade butter, you remember? Every time his mother brought it in, he'd take some out for himself. Old man Rosenstein, he always bought butter from us and Follett's, she's always had butter and eggs to sell. Just imagine, they sold her for 50 cents a roll. Look what you'd pay for it now. That was two pound rolls. I turned them in. Times have changed. They sure have. Prices are going up, still going up. I don't know where they're going to stop but maybe they'll stop somewhere. They've got to stop somewhere.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, we've got no money left.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah, well, we've got no money left. Yeah, I guess so. They keep getting debt more and more in the country so I don't know. Maybe old President Ford will get us out of them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yeah, get him out.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: One or the other. Yeah, there's an election coming up. We'll see who wins. They're sure trying to get nominated. You can read in the papers. What was that one that they shot that time? Oh well, that's politics for you. Well, if they don't like a person for the love of Mike, they don't have to vote for him but they don't have to shoot him for Pete's sake.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Crazy people.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Sure it is. It's just crazy. If I didn't want to vote for somebody, I sure as heck wouldn't be going to the Army and I wouldn't vote for him. That would hurt him worse than anything. So, maybe it'll all come out in the wash.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there much politics around here in the early days that people had elections and stuff?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: No, they didn't pay too much attention like they do now. They didn't go through all that maneuvering around.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Wouldn't take many votes to get elected from around here in the early days, I imagine.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: I can't tell you. Of course, now the farms are getting bigger and the little farmers going out. There's getting less people around living around the country now. That is actual farmers. All these farm places, their houses are rented out to people that's working other places. Moscow, Washington, some of them. So they live here but they work other place.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you find for yourself that it wasn't worth trying a farm after the depression because it took so much land and stuff? Well, yeah. What were you thinking about it?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: After I quit, I sold the farm outfit, gave my mother the money, and I went out working on farms up until I went to work at the elevator. I worked for construction, Henry George's, George and Allouay. Then I went to work down at the Farmers Union East End and I was there 25 years. Then I retired.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Wasn't the Farmers Union around here from the rather earlier days?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: It was established here in 1999. They started here at the Farmers Union. Of course, it's much bigger now. They got bigger plants and they're still building on the west end. They're putting up two more big steel botanicals down here. They're still putting the polygreen out on the site.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was it thinking from what you heard of why they started in the first place? Why did they want to have a Farmers Union?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: It was just the start of the farmers getting together in a group. That way maybe they'd get a little better price on stuff by being a group, a co-op. Well, they finally turned out to be a co-op in time. So, like Union Town's got a co-op in different places. They can, oh I don't know, I guess they get a little better price on stuff. I don't know what they really do that. So, other than that, why? They just kept building up big business, bigger running, which it is still getting that way.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Now one thing I was going to ask you about was the river going down the Clearwater there and going down the grade. Was that a fairly steep grade to get down?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yes, it was a very steep grade. They changed it to that here in the... The old grade going down, they used to have to rough lock the wagons to make sure they hold them. Really? Yeah, they didn't trust the brakes. They rough locked the wheels to get down.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you rough lock it, does that mean you...

speaker: Walter Currin
words: When you were on a train back through, it locked the wheel completely. So, you had your brake, but then sometimes they'd give away on you. That grade was awful steep. After they fixed it, after it was better before, because you know, the dirt road then. I remember the old Louisston Highway, oh my stars, that was just a winding ribbon. Yeah, it was.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You'd go down there to the river very often. There would you mostly go to Genesee.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, of course I never lived over there when that grade was going from Colton Union Town down... We used to get down the central grade here all the time in the old horse days. It'd take all day to make a trip down to Louisston and back out to the rim out here where we lived. But now then they put in the spiral highway and they keep improving that. Now they're making a new grade there now. So they've improved a lot. They're trying to get around.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about the river itself? Did you ever see that river flooding bad or trying to cross it in the flood?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, they used to have a ferry boat down here at Spalding, you know. And you went across on that before they built the old Spalding Bridge. And then, oh yeah, that would get up. It'd get up over the river, over the road going down the river. And then you'd get the ice jams. It seemed like it's been going down about, oh, we come back up here from Colton in 32. And most sides were lined up, garages and different things. Oh, 10, 12 years ago it seemed to be start sliding down. So, oh, here's Ron. Oh, my boy. That's my son-in-law. Spokane. Oh, really? Very good. Catch whitefish there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was the, what did they use to fish with?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, we used hooks and worms and stuff like that. Different things.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Because I know they used to have salmon in there and everything. Was that what you were fishing in too? Was that a pass?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah, they had salmon in there. But we'd get down there, I'd sit down there and talk with the old fellow I used to like to visit with. He had a fishing rod, he'd take fish rod and he'd take an old wooden limb. Way to go, we'd catch whitefish.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How come he took such a liking? Was it just to you that he took such a liking to you personally?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Well, he liked the...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was he going to like your folks?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, yes. He was good to the old fellow and the whole wife. The old fellow, he didn't have too good luck to his mother or mother. We'd give him some oysters to go fry and stuff like that. It didn't take much to make the old fellow happy. But he really saw a lot of us.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about the mox mox?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: I remember the old mox mox's. There was old Jim Carle and Tom Carle and Johnny Matthews and Charlie and Sam Wilson and all of them old fellas. I was around there, the old fellows, Charlie White and different ones around there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was Charlie White a baseball player?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Young Charlie was. Yeah, old Charlie was. He was only a half grade, but he farmed on the rim around here. And his dad was a white man, his mother was senior. But he was one of the finer old fellows.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Wasn't there a number of instances where there was mixed marriage like that?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, yes. There is yet. They were getting mixed up there quite a bit. Yeah. There's a lot of history down there that I don't know. I used to get it quite a bit in old Bill Patel. At first I couldn't understand him, but finally I got so active understanding him. He took a little, pretty broken English. If you got used to him, you could get used to him and you could understand him. And I liked to talk to the old fellow. He was interesting.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he like to talk about their really early days from his time?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: He was just a small boy, I guess, when old Chief Joseph made that. What I could understand, him and Suntown both, they were nephews. It's quite interesting talk to them old Indians. Of course, they had more involved. I got acquainted with them. I was kind of a pick among Indian to come by and give me stuff in the oil. We always just done a lot of good to them. We gave them stuff and liked mother give them garden stuff and all that. They didn't have money all right. They said they did all right. They repaid her back in various stuff, everything they could think about. They'd always bring her something.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When they went burying, was it usually up to who wins they win or where?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: They went up north here, up Brownville, they all would bury up in there. Huckleberry. They had some berries up in there in Clarkview. They would go up in there, camp up in there when they stayed with her or two when they come out. They'd always stop when each one of them would have a gallon of berries from her. She'd have five or six gallons of Huckleberry when she got through.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would you do with all of them?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh, she'd can them. We didn't have freezers and stuff like those days. She'd can them, everything. That's the way she kept her fruit can.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where did P.O. Potalek, he lived down on the river.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Right that way, you go down Kylie Gray.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's right, you were telling me.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: You hit the highway and right back to your right you see a little house sitting up on the point there. I guess it's descendants of his family living there now, the Reddards.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When they say the Rimrock, where does the Rimrock start?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: It starts over here about, well, where the highway junction out here, way out there, before you go hit the Uniontown. It starts there and runs through to the hill and going up here towards Juliet along the river. I don't see why that would be in here.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Pretty big district.

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh yes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it mostly being farmed by whites when you were farming it?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Yeah. Few Indians tried to farm, but they were never very good farmers. They'd just go hunting and fishing. We just mostly rented then, now a lot of them have bought the land.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where are you going to go? To the farm. Um, where's John with these plants?

speaker: Walter Currin
words: Oh sure, you can't hear.
